extracted.intended_audience: central and local government policy‑makers and regulators in Korea; regulatory reform committees; SME policy officials; ministries implementing/regulating regulatory management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and institutional standards for designing, implementing and monitoring regulatory reform in Korea, with a focus on local government roles and measures tailored to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Covers legal limits, institutional arrangements, consultation mechanisms, tailored regulation criteria, and examples of exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futuristic Regulatory Map (top-down strategic planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Futuristic Regulatory Map adopts a top-down approach to strategically establish a forward-looking framework and plan for regulatory reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected to help the government steer reform more effectively to overcome challenges such as persistence of existing regulations that hinder entry of new industries/technology and lack of necessary regulations for emerging industries. 2017 pilot: design map for self-driving cars; once methodology/procedures are developed, each central administrative agency will develop maps for other emerging industrial fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local governments' legislative authority must conform with higher law
rubrics_metrics.description: All local government regulations must be in line with higher legislation; autonomous legislative authority is prescribed in the Constitution and implemented via the Local Autonomy Act (municipal ordinance and municipal rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local governments may establish municipal ordinances concerning affairs within the scope of statutes, but matters restricting residents' rights, imposing obligations, or penalties require authority delegated by Acts (Local Autonomy Act, Article 22). Heads of local governments may establish municipal rules to the extent delegated by statutes or municipal ordinances (Article 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of local government functions (Local Autonomy Act duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments shall deal with administrative matters pertaining to welfare of local residents, manage properties, and may enact provisions relating to local autonomy within the limit of Acts and subordinate statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to the Local Autonomy Act local governments can: i) perform autonomous affairs of their jurisdiction and entrusted affairs under statutes; ii) enact or amend municipal ordinances and rules; iii) formulate and execute budgets; iv) guide and supervise policies and local affairs under subordinate agencies' jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect relationship of central vs local regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: All regulations enacted by central administrative agencies can take effect in all local regions; local regulations tailored to local characteristics are effective only within their jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies central regulation preempts or applies nationally while local rules are geographically limited; local rules must still conform to higher legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergovernmental dispute resolution procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When disputes arise between local governments, mediation is led by provincial/metropolitan heads or the Minister of the Interior, or resolved by the Central Dispute Mediation Committee; disputes between central agencies and local governments are mediated/adjusted by the Administrative Mediation Council under the Prime Minister, with unresolved matters going to the Constitutional Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional Court decisions legally bind all governmental institutions and local governments. Constitutional Court Act (Article 111, Clause 1) lists jurisdiction (constitutionality of a law upon courts' request; impeachment; dissolution of political party; competence disputes between State agencies and local governments; constitutional complaint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to register, review and improve local regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments are mandated to register regulations contained in municipal ordinances and rules, review regulations to be newly introduced or reinforced, and improve existing regulations in accordance with the central government's regulatory reform framework (Framework Act on Administrative Regulations, Article 3, Clause 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ongoing obligation to ensure local regulations are captured, assessed, and reformed consistent with national frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish local regulatory reform committees and units
rubrics_metrics.description: All local governments must establish regulatory reform committees and regulatory reform units under their jurisdiction to perform regulatory reform tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of Feb 2017 there were 613 staff across local regulatory reform units (77 in regional governments, 536 in sub-regional), with average staffing of 4–5 in regional units and 2–3 in sub-regional units. Units support internal regulatory reform committees and carry out review/improvement tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site Meetings on Regulatory Reform (quarterly engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prime Minister holds On-site Meetings on Regulatory Reform in different local regions on a quarterly basis, bringing representatives of central and local governments and business groups to discuss local regulatory reform status and action plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings focus on themed topics (examples given: creation/expansion of factories; Seven Principles on Regulatory Reform and inspection; improving restrictive regulation on competition; finalising local reform plans). Follow-up measures include 'ultimate debate on regulatory reform' and initiatives to identify and improve unreasonable local regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministry of Interior local engagement and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ministry of the Interior convenes local regulatory reform meetings with heads of local governments to address difficulties raised by businesses/citizens and ensure local regulations fall within higher legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministry conducts field visits, establishes strategic plans of local regulatory reform, and publishes annual manuals of regulatory management for local governments, which are used to form local action plans and to publish performance of reform online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial plan to identify and improve unreasonable regulations (11 major areas, three steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministerial Meeting on Regulatory Reform issued a plan (March 2015) to identify and improve unreasonable regulations across 11 major areas divided into three steps: Step 1: Land, industry, agriculture, environment, construction; Step 2: Culture and tourism, local regulations, oceans and fisheries; Step 3: Transport, health & welfare, forestry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a reform task is identified and confirmed, public consultation (e.g., joint workshops between local officials and central authorities) is conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public consultation requirement for identified reform tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation should be conducted (including joint workshops between local officials responsible for regulation and relevant central authorities) once a regulatory reform task is identified and confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation is part of the process to refine reform measures and ensure stakeholder input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and administrative measures to encourage proactive local reform
rubrics_metrics.description: The government introduced methods to promote proactive attitudes by local governments, including Pre-Audit Consulting, strengthened disciplinary standards, strengthened incentives (e.g. promotion opportunities), and expanding one-stop channels for civil complaints and licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-Audit Consulting lessens burden of ex post audits; disciplinary standards discourage passive bureaucratic attitudes; incentives aim to induce active administrative performance; one-stop channels address civil complaints/ grievances on licensing and certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME regulatory reform objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Main objective is to identify and reform SME regulations that inhibit the development of a creative economy: create a business-friendly environment for new industries/technologies, reduce regulatory barriers to start-ups, and scrutinise market regulations to facilitate sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory reform measures are targeted to reconstruct uniform/rigid standards into more rational and fair measures, taking SMEs' capabilities into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of disproportionate regulatory burden on SMEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges that around 60% of regulations pertain to SMEs and that SMEs face relatively high compliance costs and lower capacity to comply compared to large enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory costs often act as hidden taxes, aggravating burdens on SMEs. Evidence cited: compliance-cost-to-sales ratios much higher for smaller firms (e.g., 10.9% for <20 employees vs 3.3% for 100+ in 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Assessment on SMEs (RIA on SMEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: RIA on SMEs has been introduced to alleviate regulatory burdens on SMEs and enforce a tailored regulatory approach by differentiating regulatory burdens based on firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to newly established or reinforced regulations targeting SMEs; part of a broader set of SME-focused regulatory tools including on-site consultations and the SMEs Ombudsman.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site consultations with SMEs to reform existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: On-site consultation with SMEs aims to transform uniformly or rigidly managed existing regulations into more rational, flexible ones to reduce compliance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These consultations are used to identify burdensome rules and propose practical, tailored adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key success factors for SME reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying and improving unreasonable regulations through enhanced intercommunication among enterprises, improving understanding of regulatory rationale, and increasing satisfaction with regulatory reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SME satisfaction is influenced by the gap between expected and experienced qualities of reform; enhancing SMEs' understanding of reform helps strengthen investment and employment motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMEs Ombudsman role and channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The SME Ombudsman serves as a medium for intercommunication among enterprises and as a platform to identify burdensome regulations; operates in 243 local governments with small-scale meetings at least weekly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ombudsman channels receive complaints and help resolve on-site difficulties; statistics show many complaints resolved (example: 9,855 resolved out of 10,150 submitted since establishment in 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: SME classification criteria (post-2015: average annual sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2015 SMEs are classified based on average sales over the past three years; industry-specific ceilings are applied to ensure sector characteristics are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different sectors have different average annual sales ceilings (examples: some manufacturing sectors < KRW 150 billion; other sectors have thresholds of KRW 100b, 80b, 60b, 40b). Micro enterprise status determined by number of full-time employees (sector-specific: <10 or <5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailored regulatory approach for SMEs (differentiation factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each regulation differentiates regulatory compliance costs according to factors such as enterprise classification, sales, number of full-time employees, equity capital and construction expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: micro enterprises (<10 FT employees) exempt from certain reporting/ employment rule drafting; IT firms with annual sales under KRW 10 billion exempt from mandatory ISMS certification; firms with gross capital < KRW 10 billion exempt from external audit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit exemptions and reduced obligations for micro/small firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific statutory exemptions apply to micro and small enterprises (examples across Acts):
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labour Standards Act: micro enterprises (<10 FT employees) exempt from obligation to report or draft employment rules; Employment Insurance reporting may allow written rather than electronic records for micro firms; Act on Employment Promotion and Vocational Rehabilitation for Disabled Persons: small enterprises (<50 FT employees) exempt from duty of hiring disabled persons; Occupational Safety and Health Act: small enterprises (<50 FT employees in manufacturing) exempt from duty to establish/operate an occupational safety and health committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary exemption period for newly implemented tailored regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once tailored regulations are implemented, micro enterprises with less than 10 full-time employees are, in principle, exempted from regulations for 3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tailored Regulatory Approach for SMEs is officially included in the Ordinance of the Prime Minister; other necessary measures (e.g., less burdensome regulations) are considered to reduce burdens on small enterprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic and ancillary criteria catalog for tailoring regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic criteria for implementing tailored regulatory approaches include full-time employees, sales and equity capital; ancillary criteria include construction expenses, building area, emission quantity and tonnage of a vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table examples: firms employing fewer than 500 employees may be exempt from some obligations (e.g., mandatory workplace child care facilities); exemptions may be tied to pollutant emission volumes, building area, or construction expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector‑specific numerical thresholds for SME/small business status
rubrics_metrics.description: Sector tables define industry codes and corresponding size standards (average annual sales thresholds for SMEs and small business categories, e.g., KRW 150b, 100b, 80b, 60b, 40b for SMEs; KRW 12b, 8b, 5b, 3b, 1b for small businesses depending on sector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry classification follows Korea Standard Industrial Classification (KSIC) and statutory articles (Article 2 of Framework Act on SMEs and Article 3 of Enforcement Decree). These thresholds guide eligibility for tailored measures and exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential treatment mechanics (examples of application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples demonstrating how tailored criteria are applied to specific statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: micro enterprises allowed written reporting instead of electronic for insurance premium collection; IT firms under sales thresholds exempt from ISMS certification; small enterprises under thresholds exempt from mandatory committees or hiring duties under specific Acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance targets and numerical reduction goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of quantitative targets for regulatory reduction (example: in 2014 each central administrative agency initiated a regulatory reduction program to decrease unreasonable economic regulations by 10%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each central administrative agency set its own targets; example result: 995 out of 9,876 regulations pertaining to investment promotion, mitigation of burdens, and alleviation of administrative burdens for SMEs were reformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, complaint channels and publication of reform performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments should regularly publish the performance of their reform work online and operate channels (regulatory petition centres, SME Ombudsman) to collect and resolve complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: regulatory petition centres operate within 243 local governments; SMEs Ombudsman holds weekly small-scale meetings; complaint statistics reported (e.g., 10,150 complaints submitted since 2009 with 9,855 resolved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical reform pathways as precedent for future measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Past reform measures provide a menu of options: abolishing large numbers of regulations, temporary regulatory suspension, easing capital/ certification requirements for start-ups, simplifying procedures, easing bidding restrictions for SME procurement, lowering thresholds for entrepreneurial ventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These historical examples indicate feasible reform instruments (revocation of minimum capital requirements, temporary suspensions, exemption programs, procurement liberalisation) that can be applied in future SME reform efforts.
